description: Solo builder looking for teammates for Field Shift. I’m a biotech researcher working on domestic yak in Northern Pakistan, building a NASA-data tool that helps yak herders in Gilgit-Baltistan compare grazing-rotation strategies (which pasture to graze, rest, and when to move), with advice sent by SMS. Plan and requirements are ready. Looking for: Python/data, remote sensing (MODIS, NDVI), Streamlit or web frontend, and slides/design. Virtual, PKT.
summary: PasturePulse is a grazing-rotation decision-support tool for yak herders in Shimshal, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. Herders there move their animals between spring and summer pastures by a fixed calendar, but shifting snowmelt, green-up and summer heat no longer follow that calendar, and most high pastures have no internet. The tool downloads 25 years of NASA POWER climate data and MODIS vegetation and snow data to compare three rotation strategies (the existing calendar, moves timed to each year's snowmelt and green-up, and climate-timed moves with rest-rotation of pasture blocks) and to compute three daily signals: yak heat stress, forage condition and upper-pasture readiness. The tool turns the chosen strategy into a one-line SMS in Roman Urdu that tells the herder which pasture to use and what to do, and sends nothing when data is missing. This answers the Field Shift challenge by applying rotation thinking to pasture land: which pasture to graze, which to rest and when to move, to protect pasture cover and adapt herding to a changing climate.
details:
What it does

PasturePulse helps yak-herding families and extension workers answer three practical questions: is the upper pasture ready, is this season's grass below normal, and is heat a risk this week? It then compares three ways of rotating herds between pastures and turns the result into simple SMS advice.

  1. Compare rotation strategies (2001–2025). For each strategy the tool shows its rule, why it is suggested, the evidence from NASA data, its benefits, information gaps, and risks that need local review:
    • Existing calendar: move up and down on fixed dates, as herders do now.
    • Climate-timed: move up when the upper pasture is snow-free and greening; move down when greenness falls or snow returns.
    • Climate-timed + rest-rotation: graze the upper block with better vegetation cover and rest the other, to let vegetation and soil recover. The herder or extension worker picks a main goal (right timing, less heat stress, protect pasture cover, or least effort), and the strategies are ranked with the weights shown on screen.
    • Heat stress: the yak Temperature-Humidity Index (THI) from Krishnan et al. (2009). Yaks feel heat stress above THI 52, far below the cattle threshold of 72.
    • Forage condition: the Vegetation Condition Index, comparing current MODIS NDVI with the same 16-day period in earlier years.
    • Migration readiness: the upper pasture is snow-free (MODIS snow/ice flag), greening, and not past its usual peak.
  2. SMS advice. The message names the pasture and one action, fits one SMS (160 characters), contains no technical terms, matches the exact cause (snow versus slow green-up) and depends on where the herd currently is.

How it works

  • Data: NASA POWER daily air temperature and humidity; MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI and pixel reliability at 250 m every 16 days, for three pasture points chosen on satellite imagery.
  • Temperature is corrected from the NASA POWER grid to pasture elevation with a lapse rate, and humidity is recomputed by holding vapour pressure constant.
  • Every baseline uses only earlier years, so past evaluations do not use future data.
  • Trends in snow-off, green-up and peak dates are tested with Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test.
  • All alerts come from transparent rules; every threshold is shown with its source, and our own starting values are labelled "team default".

Benefits

  • Advice reaches herders on basic phones without internet.
  • Herders keep the decision: the tool shows evidence and trade-offs, it does not replace their judgment.
  • Rest-rotation evidence supports protecting pasture cover and soil on fragile high-altitude rangeland.

What we hope to achieve

A pilot with herders in Shimshal to check the thresholds against their experience, followed by NISAR radar data for snow under cloud, messages in Urdu, Wakhi and Burushaski, and two-way SMS so herders can report conditions back.

Limitations

NASA POWER is coarse (about 0.5 degrees); MODIS 250 m pixels can mix pasture with rock in narrow valleys; the yak THI limit comes from one study site in India; pasture locations and move dates are estimates until checked with herders; SMS sending is simulated in this prototype.

In this hackathon prototype the code is written and unit-tested, but the full run on real data for the final pasture locations was not completed before the deadline, so we report no results yet.

Tools

Python, pandas, NumPy, Streamlit, requests, pytest; NASA POWER API; ORNL DAAC MODIS web service; Google Earth for choosing pasture locations; GitHub.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), daily point data: T2M (air temperature at 2 m) and RH2M (relative humidity at 2 m), 2001–2025, accessed through the POWER API.
MODIS Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day 250 m (MOD13Q1, version 6.1): NDVI and pixel reliability (used as a snow/ice flag), 2001–2025, accessed through the ORNL DAAC MODIS web service.
